newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia plane maker threatens paper over crash.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia plane maker threatens paper over crash.

text.p: Indonesian authorities said on Tuesday that a faulty parachute cord triggered the crash of a locally made military plane last month, killing all six people on board.

The findings have prompted the state-owned plane maker Industri Pesawat Terbang Nusantara (IPTN) to publicly threaten a local English-language newspaper, the Jakarta Post, with legal action over its incorrect report on the accident.

In a detailed explanation at a press briefing that appeared aimed at reassuring potential foreign buyers of the plane, military officials said the twin-engined turbo-prop CN-235-220 military aircraft crashed as a result of a chain reaction started by a parachute cord snapping during a low-altitude test flight.

The press briefing, unprecedented for Indonesia's usually tight-lipped military, came only a few weeks before the country planned to display a similar maritime patrol aircraft and its latest home-grown N-250 commuter plane at the Paris Air Show.

"There was no sign of a fault in either the aircraft, the aircraft's systems or the test procedures used by the aircraft's crew," said Air Force Lieutenant-Colonel Syarkiputeh, head of the team that investigated the crash.

A senior defence department official said the unusual openness about the crash of the CN-235, jointly designed with CASA of Spain as a 44-seat passenger aircraft with both military and civilian models, was to protect Indonesia's reputation as it seeks foreign buyers.
"We have had to be open because this is our national plane and we want to sell it overseas," said the official, who asked not to be named.
The military version of the CN-235, made by IPTN and flown by the country's most experienced test pilot, Erwin Danuwinata, crashed on May 22 at the Gorda military airfield near Serang in West Java.

Lawyers for IPTN told a news conference the firm feared it could lose contracts worth up to $300 million in the United Arab Emirates, South Korea and Australia after the Jakarta Post report was reprinted in Singapore and a number of Middle East newspapers.

"From the video made by the chaser plane and an IPTN crew on the ground there was no evidence to support what was mentioned by the Jakarta Post," lawyer Adnan Buyung Nasution, head of IPTN's legal team, said.

The front-page story, retracted the following day, had quoted IPTN sources as saying "smoke billowed from the fuselage" in the moments before the crash and "there were indications that one of the plane's propellers broke off before the fire started".

IPTN, controlled by high-profile Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie, released a video of the crash for broadcast last month showing the pilot struggling to regain control and no smoke until the plane burst into flames on impact.
Nasution said IPTN had asked the newspaper to publish apologies around the world for its mistake and pay undisclosed damages within seven days or face legal action.

Raymond Toruan, business manager of the Jakarta Post, told Reuters the paper had not yet made a decision but noted it had already apologised for the mistake "without malice" and had taken internal action.
Syarkiputeh said the accident occurred during a High Altitude Parachute Extraction System (HAPES) test as the aircraft was flying at 1,100 feet with a four-tonne test load of sand.
He said the cord tying the two small extraction parachutes to the test load broke after being deployed, causing a sudden shift in the centre of balance of the plane.
"The shifting of the centre of balance of the aircraft caused it to become unstable and crash. The low altitude made it impossible for the pilot to take emergency action," he added.
